subject: biology
title: Microbes in Human Welfare
subtitle: Microbes in household and industrial products, sewage treatment, biogas production, and microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilisers

seo.meta_description: NEET Biology — Microbes in Human Welfare: microbes in curd, bread and fermented foods, industrial products (antibiotics, alcohol, organic acids, enzymes), sewage treatment and the activated-sludge process, biogas production, and microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilisers, with NEET-level examples and MCQs. Free on Vidaara.

summary:
• Household: curd (Lactobacillus/LAB), dough & bread (yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae), cheese (Swiss = Propionibacterium; Roquefort = Penicillium).
  • Industrial: ethanol/wine/beer (yeast), antibiotics (penicillin — Penicillium notatum, by Fleming), organic acids (citric — Aspergillus niger), enzymes (lipase, pectinase, streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins).
  • Sewage treatment: primary (physical) then secondary/biological — activated sludge (aerobic flocs) → anaerobic sludge digesters producing biogas.
  • Biogas: mixture (mainly methane) made by methanogens (e.g. Methanobacterium) from dung/waste.
  • Biocontrol: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), Trichoderma, Baculoviruses (NPV); ladybird, dragonfly.
  • Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Azospirillum, cyanobacteria (Anabaena), mycorrhiza (Glomus).

faqs.q: Which microbes are used to make curd, bread and cheese?
faqs.a: Curd is made by lactic acid bacteria (LAB) such as Lactobacillus, which coagulate and partially digest milk proteins. Bread (and the rising of dough) uses baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which produces CO2. Cheeses use various microbes for flavour and texture — for example, the large holes in Swiss cheese are due to CO2 from Propionibacterium sharmanii, and Roquefort cheese is ripened with the fungus Penicillium roqueforti.

faqs.q: What are antibiotics and which microbe produced the first one?
faqs.a: Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by some microbes that can kill or stop the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes. The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the mould Penicillium notatum; it was later developed as a drug by Chain and Florey. Antibiotics revolutionised the treatment of bacterial diseases.

Sewage is treated in two main stages. Primary treatment physically removes solids by filtration and sedimentation. Secondary (biological) treatment uses aerobic microbes that form 'flocs' to consume the organic matter, greatly reducing the BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) — this is the activated-sludge process. The settled sludge is then digested by anaerobic bacteria, which produce biogas, and the treated water is released.

faqs.q: What is biogas and which microbes produce it?
faqs.a: Biogas is a mixture of gases (mainly methane, with CO2 and H2S) produced by the anaerobic breakdown of organic matter such as cattle dung ('gobar'). It is produced by methanogens — methane-producing bacteria like Methanobacterium — which also live in the rumen of cattle and in anaerobic sludge. Biogas is used as fuel for cooking and lighting.

faqs.q: What are biofertilisers and biocontrol agents?
faqs.a: Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich soil nutrients naturally — for example Rhizobium (fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules), free-living Azospirillum and Azotobacter, cyanobacteria like Anabaena, and mycorrhizal fungi (Glomus) that help roots absorb phosphorus. Biocontrol agents are organisms used to control pests and diseases instead of chemicals — for example Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) against insect larvae, the fungus Trichoderma against plant pathogens, and ladybirds against aphids.

modules.title: Microbes in Household and Industrial Products

topics.title: Microbes in Household Products
topics.concept:
Microbes are not only agents of disease — they are enormously useful, and many work quietly in our own kitchens. A classic example is curd. It is made from milk by lactic acid bacteria (LAB), chiefly Lactobacillus: a small amount of curd (the 'starter' or inoculum) added to warm milk multiplies and produces lactic acid, which coagulates and partially digests the milk proteins. LAB also increase vitamin B12 in the curd and, in the stomach, help check disease-causing microbes.

The dough used to make bread, dosa and idli is also fermented by microbes. For idli and dosa the batter is fermented by LAB, while the puffiness of bread comes from baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), which releases carbon dioxide that makes the dough rise.

Cheese is one of the oldest microbial products, and different microbes give different cheeses their character — a popular NEET fact. The large holes in 'Swiss cheese' are produced by a large amount of CO₂ released by a bacterium, Propionibacterium sharmanii. The 'Roquefort cheese' is ripened by growing a specific fungus, Penicillium roqueforti, on it, which gives a particular flavour.

Many traditional foods of the world are likewise fermented, such as the South Indian foods and the Bharuch (Gujarat) drink, and 'toddy' is a traditional fermented drink made from sap of palms. The common thread is that helpful microbes — mainly bacteria and yeasts — transform simple ingredients into nutritious, flavourful products. For NEET, fix the microbe for each product: curd = LAB/Lactobacillus; bread dough rising = yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae); Swiss cheese holes = Propionibacterium (CO₂); Roquefort cheese = Penicillium.

examples.problem: Which microbe sets curd from milk, and what does it produce that coagulates the milk?
examples.solution: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB), mainly Lactobacillus, set curd. They produce lactic acid, which coagulates and partially digests the milk proteins (and also increases vitamin B12).

examples.problem: What causes the large holes in Swiss cheese?
examples.solution: The large holes are due to the production of a large amount of carbon dioxide (CO₂) by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii during ripening.

quiz.q: The rising of bread dough is due to:
quiz.explanation: Baker's yeast releases CO₂, making the dough rise.

quiz.q: The holes in Swiss cheese are due to CO₂ from:

quiz.explanation: The fungus Penicillium roqueforti ripens Roquefort cheese.

topics.note: NEET tip: Curd = LAB/Lactobacillus (lactic acid; ↑ B12). Bread dough rises by yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (CO₂). Swiss cheese holes = Propionibacterium (CO₂); Roquefort = fungus Penicillium.

topics.title: Microbes in Industrial Products
topics.concept:
On an industrial scale, microbes are grown in large vessels called fermentors (bioreactors) to make valuable products. One of the oldest uses is making fermented (alcoholic) beverages. The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (called brewer's yeast here) ferments sugars to ethanol. Wine and beer are produced without distillation, whereas whisky, brandy and rum are produced by distillation of the fermented broth.

The most important medical products are antibiotics — chemicals made by microbes that kill or stop other microbes. The story begins with Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin from the mould Penicillium notatum (its full potential as a drug was later established by Chain and Florey). Penicillin was used widely to treat wounded soldiers in World War II, and antibiotics have since transformed medicine.

Microbes also yield useful organic acids, enzymes and other bioactive molecules. Organic acids include citric acid (Aspergillus niger), acetic acid (Acetobacter aceti), butyric acid (Clostridium butylicum) and lactic acid (Lactobacillus). Industrially important enzymes include lipases (used in detergents to remove oily stains), pectinases (to clarify bottled juices) and streptokinase (from Streptococcus, used as a 'clot buster' to dissolve blood clots in heart-attack patients).

Two other named bioactive molecules are frequently asked. Cyclosporin A, from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, is used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants. Statins, produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus, are used to lower blood cholesterol (they block an enzyme in cholesterol synthesis). For NEET, fix the alcohol products (with/without distillation), penicillin (Fleming, Penicillium notatum), citric acid (Aspergillus niger), streptokinase (clot buster), cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant) and statins (cholesterol-lowering).

examples.problem: Differentiate the production of wine from that of whisky.
examples.solution: Wine (and beer) is produced without distillation of the fermented broth, while whisky (and brandy, rum) is produced with distillation of the fermented broth (giving a higher alcohol content). Both use the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

examples.problem: Name the microbe and use of (i) streptokinase and (ii) cyclosporin A.
examples.solution: (i) Streptokinase is produced by Streptococcus and used as a 'clot buster' to dissolve blood clots. (ii) Cyclosporin A is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum and used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants.

quiz.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium notatum.
Wine/beer are made without distillation; whisky/rum with distillation.

quiz.q: Statins, which lower blood cholesterol, are produced by:
quiz.explanation: Statins come from the yeast Monascus purpureus.

topics.note: NEET tip: Yeast Saccharomyces → ethanol; wine/beer (no distillation) vs whisky/rum (distillation). Penicillin = Penicillium notatum (Fleming). Citric acid = Aspergillus niger. Streptokinase = clot buster; cyclosporin A (Trichoderma) = immunosuppressant; statins (Monascus) = cholesterol-lowering.

modules.title: Microbes in Sewage, Energy and Agriculture

topics.title: Sewage Treatment and Biogas Production
topics.concept:
Cities produce huge amounts of sewage (municipal waste water), rich in organic matter and microbes. It cannot be released into rivers directly, so it is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) using heterotrophic microbes, in two main stages.

Primary treatment is essentially physical: the sewage is passed through filters and grit chambers to remove floating debris and grit, and then allowed to settle so that the solids form the primary sludge while the supernatant forms the effluent. Secondary (biological) treatment then acts on this effluent. It is passed into large aeration tanks where it is constantly agitated and air is pumped in; this lets useful aerobic microbes grow into masses called 'flocs' (mesh-like bacterial colonies). These microbes consume the organic matter, drastically reducing the BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) of the water — a lower BOD means cleaner water. This is the activated-sludge process.

Once the BOD is low, the sewage is passed to settling tanks where the bacterial flocs sediment as the activated sludge; a part of this is used as the inoculum for the next batch, and the rest is pumped into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters. Here other, anaerobic bacteria digest the sludge, producing a mixture of gases including methane — biogas.

This links directly to biogas production. Biogas is a mixture of gases (predominantly methane, with CO₂ and H₂S) produced by the anaerobic breakdown of organic matter. The microbes responsible are the methanogens — methane-producing bacteria such as Methanobacterium — which also occur in the rumen of cattle (so cattle dung, 'gobar', is rich in them). In a biogas (gobar gas) plant, dung slurry is digested anaerobically to release biogas used as fuel for cooking and lighting, and the spent slurry is used as manure. For NEET, fix the two stages of sewage treatment (primary = physical; secondary = activated-sludge, lowers BOD) and biogas (methane, methanogens like Methanobacterium, cattle rumen/dung).

examples.problem: What is BOD, and how does the activated-sludge process change it?
examples.solution: BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed by microbes to break down the organic matter in water — a measure of organic pollution. In the activated-sludge process, aerobic microbes consume the organic matter, so the BOD falls sharply, indicating the water is now much cleaner.

examples.problem: Which microbes produce biogas, and why is cattle dung used in biogas plants?
examples.solution: Biogas is produced by methanogens (methane-producing bacteria, e.g. Methanobacterium). Cattle dung is used because these bacteria are abundant in the rumen of cattle, so dung ('gobar') is naturally rich in methanogens.

quiz.explanation: It lowers the BOD, indicating cleaner water.

quiz.q: The main combustible gas in biogas is:

quiz.explanation: They occur in the rumen of cattle (hence dung is used).

topics.note: NEET tip: Sewage: primary = physical (settling); secondary = biological activated-sludge (aerobic flocs lower BOD). Sludge → anaerobic digesters → biogas. Biogas = mainly methane, made by methanogens (Methanobacterium); abundant in cattle rumen → dung-based 'gobar gas' plants.

topics.title: Microbes as Biocontrol Agents and Biofertilisers
topics.concept:
Modern agriculture is moving away from harmful chemicals toward biological methods, and microbes are central to this. Biological control (biocontrol) is the use of living organisms to control plant pests and diseases instead of chemical pesticides — this protects beneficial insects and reduces pollution.

Several biocontrol agents are heavily examined. The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) produces a protein toxin that kills the larvae of certain insects; it is sprayed as a powder, and its toxin gene has also been introduced into crops to make Bt cotton. The fungus Trichoderma is a free-living fungus used to control several plant pathogens (it protects the roots). Baculoviruses (genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus, NPV) are used as narrow-spectrum (species-specific) insecticides that do not harm other organisms. Among animals, the ladybird beetle controls aphids and dragonflies control mosquitoes.

Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil, mainly by adding nitrogen and helping with phosphorus — a clean alternative to chemical fertilisers. The most important nitrogen-fixers are the bacteria. Rhizobium lives symbiotically in the root nodules of legumes and fixes atmospheric nitrogen; Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil.

Other groups also act as biofertilisers. Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria fix nitrogen and are especially important in paddy fields (the water fern Azolla with Anabaena is a famous biofertiliser for rice). Finally, the fungal symbiosis called mycorrhiza — especially the genus Glomus — associates with plant roots and helps absorb phosphorus (and gives tolerance to drought and disease). For NEET, fix the biocontrol agents (Bt against larvae, Trichoderma against pathogens, baculovirus/NPV species-specific) and the biofertilisers (Rhizobium symbiotic, Azospirillum/Azotobacter free-living, cyanobacteria in paddy, mycorrhiza/Glomus for phosphorus).

examples.problem: How does Bacillus thuringiensis act as a biocontrol agent?
examples.solution: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) produces a protein toxin that, when eaten by certain insect larvae, kills them. It is applied as a spray (or its toxin gene is engineered into crops like Bt cotton), controlling pests without broad chemical pesticides.

examples.problem: Name a symbiotic and a free-living nitrogen-fixing biofertiliser, and the fungus that helps in phosphorus uptake.
examples.solution: Symbiotic N-fixer: Rhizobium (in legume root nodules). Free-living N-fixer: Azospirillum or Azotobacter. The mycorrhizal fungus Glomus helps the plant absorb phosphorus.

quiz.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis produces the Bt insecticidal toxin.
Rhizobium is symbiotic in legume root nodules.

topics.note: NEET tip: Biocontrol: Bt (insect larvae), Trichoderma (plant pathogens), baculovirus/NPV (species-specific), ladybird→aphids, dragonfly→mosquito. Biofertilisers: Rhizobium (symbiotic N-fix, legumes), Azospirillum/Azotobacter (free-living), cyanobacteria (Anabaena, paddy), mycorrhiza Glomus (phosphorus).

questions.q: The CO₂ that makes bread dough rise comes from:

questions.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium notatum.
Rhizobium fixes nitrogen symbiotically in legume nodules.
Cyclosporin A (from Trichoderma) is an immunosuppressant.

questions.q:
A: Baker's yeast makes bread soft and puffy.
R: Yeast ferments sugars and releases carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise.
options: Both A and R true, R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.explanation: CO₂ from fermentation is exactly what makes the dough rise — R explains A.

questions.q:
A: A lower BOD indicates cleaner water.
R: BOD measures the oxygen microbes would need to break down organic matter, so less organic pollution means a lower BOD.
options: Both A and R true, R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.explanation: Less organic matter → lower oxygen demand → lower BOD — R explains A.

questions.q:
A: Biogas is produced under anaerobic conditions.
R: Methanogens, which generate the methane in biogas, are anaerobic bacteria.
options: Both A and R true, R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.explanation: Methanogens being anaerobic is exactly why biogas forms anaerobically — R explains A.

questions.q:
A: Rhizobium increases soil nitrogen.
R: It fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants.
options: Both A and R true, R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.explanation: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation is why it enriches soil nitrogen — R explains A.
